_meta: A store of existing keys plus a sequence of lookups (some for keys that do not exist, several of them repeated), used to show why a cache that stores only hits lets repeated lookups of a MISSING key hit the origin every time, and why the cache must also store the misses -- negative caching. A read-through cache normally works like this: on a lookup, return the cached value if present; otherwise call the origin (the database or backing service), and if the origin returns a value, cache it. The unstated assumption is that every lookup eventually finds a value to cache. It does not: many lookups are for keys that do not exist -- a mistyped URL, a deleted record, a probe for ids that were never issued, a scraper walking a range. For those keys the origin returns 'not found', there is nothing to cache, so the next lookup of the same missing key misses the cache again and hits the origin again. A key that is requested a thousand times and does not exist becomes a thousand origin calls -- the cache protects the origin for hits but not for misses, and a flood of missing-key requests (accidental or malicious, called cache penetration) sails straight through to the backing store. Negative caching fixes this by caching the ABSENCE too: when the origin says 'not found', store a marker for that key so subsequent lookups of the same missing key are served from the cache, and every key -- present or absent -- costs at most one origin call. store is the set of keys that exist in the origin; lookups is the sequence of keys requested, in order. store and lookups are the fixture; the origin-call counts under each policy, and which lookups hit the origin, are computed.
